clinicalPearls: The commonest non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of childhood, typically presenting in infancy as one or a few firm yellow-orange to reddish-brown papules or nodules on the head, neck or upper trunk.
Solitary lesions predominate; most appear within the first year of life and a proportion are congenital.
The majority are cutaneous and self-limiting, involuting spontaneously over months to a few years, often leaving atrophy or hyperpigmentation.

Ocular involvement, most often unilateral iris disease, is the commonest extracutaneous site and may cause spontaneous hyphaema, glaucoma or visual loss; young children with skin lesions warrant ophthalmological vigilance.

An association with neurofibromatosis type 1 and, in a subset, with juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (the classic triple association) should prompt review of café-au-lait macules and full blood count.

Histology shows a dermal infiltrate of foamy histiocytes with characteristic Touton giant cells; lesions are CD68 and factor XIIIa positive but CD1a and langerin (CD207) negative, distinguishing them from Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
Systemic or visceral disease (liver, lung, central nervous system) is rare and occurs mainly in infants with multiple cutaneous lesions.
Reassurance and observation suffice for uncomplicated skin disease; intervention is reserved for symptomatic ocular or systemic involvement.
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a benign proliferative disorder of the mononuclear phagocyte system, classified among the non-Langerhans cell (so-called C group / cutaneous) histiocytoses. The lesional cell is a dermal dendrocyte-derived histiocyte that accumulates lipid to produce the characteristic foamy, xanthomatous appearance despite normal serum lipids. The infiltrate is composed of histiocytes expressing macrophage markers such as CD68, CD163 and factor XIIIa but lacking the Langerhans cell markers CD1a and langerin, and Touton giant cells with a wreath of nuclei surrounding a central eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripheral foamy rim are typical. The proliferation is thought to represent a reactive granulomatous response of dermal dendrocytes rather than a clonal neoplasm in most cases, which accords with its usual self-limiting behaviour and spontaneous involution as lipidised histiocytes are cleared.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry (CD68, factor XIIIa, CD1a, langerin)
Slit-lamp ophthalmological examination when ocular symptoms or multiple lesions in young children
Full blood count and blood film to screen for juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia in at-risk infants
Examination for café-au-lait macules and features of neurofibromatosis type 1
Serum lipid profile to exclude hyperlipidaemic xanthoma when clinically indicated
Imaging (ultrasound, MRI) if visceral or central nervous system involvement is suspected
Dermoscopy showing the characteristic setting-sun or clouds pattern as an adjunct
redFlags: New ocular symptoms such as a red eye, spontaneous hyphaema or raised intraocular pressure suggesting iris involvement
Multiple cutaneous lesions in an infant, which increase the likelihood of ocular or systemic disease
Hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias or a leukaemoid blood picture suggesting juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia
Neurological signs or a mass suggesting central nervous system or visceral xanthogranuloma
Café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling indicating coexistent neurofibromatosis type 1
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous prognosis is excellent, with most solitary lesions involuting spontaneously over months to a few years leaving little or no residual change. Ocular and systemic disease carries greater morbidity and requires specialist management, but life-threatening visceral involvement is uncommon.
pitfalls: Mistaking juvenile xanthogranuloma for Langerhans cell histiocytosis; immunohistochemistry for CD1a and langerin resolves the distinction.
Overlooking asymptomatic ocular involvement in a young child with multiple skin lesions and thereby missing preventable visual loss.
Assuming all yellowish paediatric papules reflect hyperlipidaemia and ordering unnecessary lipid work-up for lesions that are histologically classic.
Failing to screen for neurofibromatosis type 1 and juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia in children with the recognised triple association.
Recommending disfiguring excision of a lesion destined to involute spontaneously.
references: WHO Classification of Histiocytoses and revised histiocytosis classification (current)
Standard paediatric dermatology reference texts (current editions)
management: Observe and reassure for solitary cutaneous lesions, as most involute spontaneously over months to a few years
Reserve surgical excision for symptomatic, diagnostically uncertain or functionally troublesome lesions
Undertake slit-lamp ophthalmological surveillance for iris disease, treating ocular involvement with topical or intraocular corticosteroids and managing hyphaema or glaucoma
Screen at-risk infants for juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia with full blood count and film and examine for neurofibromatosis type 1 café-au-lait macules
Manage systemic or visceral disease with chemotherapy under paediatric haematology-oncology guidance
Coordinate multidisciplinary dermatology, ophthalmology and haematology input for extracutaneous disease
